Author

Angelina Cravey-Taylor

Published

June 7, 2026

Introduction / Study Overview

This reproducible report documents the data preparation, variable construction, descriptive statistics, primary analyses, and figures for this study.

The report is intended to accompany a manuscript-style research paper. The report cannot substitute the full paper itself. Rather, this displays a transparent record of the reported results, using a reproducible Quarto workflow.

This study examined whether communication style and attachment security influence social attraction and perceived relationship compatibility, and their interaction.

The design included one manipulated independent variable and one quasi-categorical moderator :

- communication condition: low communication profile versus high communication profile

- attachment security: lower attachment security versus higher attachment security

The dependent variables were social attraction scores and perceived compatibility scores.

The primary analyses tested whether communication condition, attachment security, and their interaction predicted social attraction and perceived compatibility.

It was predicted that participants in the high communication condition would report greater social attraction and perceived compatibility than those in the low communication condition. Furthermore, attachment security was predicted to moderate this effect, such that individuals with higher attachment security would report greater attraction and compatibility in response to the high communication profile; whereas individuals with lower attachment security would show less variation in responses across the communication profiles.

Setup and Software Environment

This section loads the packages used for data preparation, scale construction, statistical modeling, estimated marginal means, and figures.

Load Packages

Show code 
library(tidyverse)  # data manipulation + plotting
library(psych)      # scale construction + reliability
library(afex)       # ANOVA models + effect sizes
library(emmeans)    # estimated marginal means + confidence intervals

Data Source

The dataset was imported from the project ‘data’ folder. The imported dataset was saved as ‘study_raw’ so that the original file remained unchanged throughout the report.

A smaller analysis dataset was created for the current analyses. This dataset retained the study condition variables, demographic variables, attachment security items, social attraction items, and perceived compatibility items needed for variable preparation and analysis.

Variable Preparation and Scale Construction

This section prepares the variables used in the primary analyses. The original imported dataset was unchanged; all prepared variables were created in the ‘study_data’ working analysis dataset.

Prepare Participant ID and Experimental Condition

Show code 
study_data <- study_data %>%
  mutate(
    id = row_number(),
    condition = factor(
      condition,
      levels = c(0, 1),
      labels = c("Low", "High")
    )
  )

The experimetal communication condition variable was recoded as a labeled factor with two levels: Low and High. Participant ID variable was also created so that every row of the dataset had a unique identifier.

Reverse-Code Scale Items

Items requiring reverse coding were adjusted prior to scale scores being computed. Given that this study included three Likert scales with different response ranges, reverse-coded items were created by subtracting each item response from the respective scale maximum plus one (i.e., 8 for 1-7 scales and 7 for 1-6 scales).

Show code 
study_data <- study_data %>%
  mutate(
    IAS_3r = 8 - IAS_3,
    IAS_4r = 8 - IAS_4,
    IAS_5r = 8 - IAS_5,
    
    ETTR_2r  = 7 - ETTR_2,
    ETTR_5r  = 7 - ETTR_5,
    ETTR_7r  = 7 - ETTR_7,
    ETTR_10r = 7 - ETTR_10,
    ETTR_13r = 7 - ETTR_13,
    ETTR_16r = 7 - ETTR_16,
    ETTR_18r = 7 - ETTR_18,
    
    AAS_8r  = 6 - AAS_8,
    AAS_13r = 6 - AAS_13,
    AAS_17r = 6 - AAS_17,
    AAS_2r  = 6 - AAS_2,
    AAS_16r = 6 - AAS_16,
    AAS_18r = 6 - AAS_18,
    
    AAS_3r  = 6 - AAS_3,
    AAS_4r  = 6 - AAS_4,
    AAS_9r  = 6 - AAS_9,
    AAS_10r = 6 - AAS_10,
    AAS_11r = 6 - AAS_11,
    AAS_15r = 6 - AAS_15
  )

Create Scale Scores

Scale item lists were defined and used to compute attachment security, social attraction, and perceived compatibility scores.

Note: AAS items were reverse-scored so that all attachment scale scores point in a positive direction. Higher scores indicate more adaptive attachment-related outcomes. Specifically, higher total AAS scores indicate higher overall attachment security, higher closeness scores indicate greater comfort with closeness, higher dependence scores indicate greater comfort depending on others, and higher anxiety-security scores indicate lower attachment anxiety.

Show code 
# Define IAS social attraction items
IAS_items <- c("IAS_1", "IAS_2", "IAS_3r", "IAS_4r", "IAS_5r", "IAS_6")

# Define revised AAS close, depend, and anxiety-security items
aas_close_items <- c("AAS_1", "AAS_6", "AAS_8r", "AAS_12", "AAS_13r", "AAS_17r")

aas_depend_items <- c("AAS_2r", "AAS_5", "AAS_7", "AAS_14", "AAS_16r", "AAS_18r")

aas_anxiety_items <- c("AAS_3r", "AAS_4r", "AAS_9r", "AAS_10r", "AAS_11r", "AAS_15r")

aas_total_items <- c(aas_close_items, aas_depend_items, aas_anxiety_items)

# Define ETRR relationship expectation items
ETTR_items <- c("ETTR_1", "ETTR_2r", "ETTR_3", "ETTR_4", "ETTR_5r", "ETTR_6", 
                "ETTR_7r", "ETTR_8", "ETTR_9", "ETTR_10r", "ETTR_11", "ETTR_12", 
                "ETTR_13r", "ETTR_14", "ETTR_15", "ETTR_16r", "ETTR_17", "ETTR_18r", "ETTR_19")

study_data <- study_data %>%
  mutate(
    IAS_scale = rowMeans(across(all_of(IAS_items)), na.rm = TRUE),
    aas_close_scale = rowMeans(across(all_of(aas_close_items)), na.rm = TRUE),
    aas_depend_scale = rowMeans(across(all_of(aas_depend_items)), na.rm = TRUE),
    aas_anxiety_scale = rowMeans(across(all_of(aas_anxiety_items)), na.rm = TRUE),
    aas_total_scale = rowMeans(across(all_of(aas_total_items)), na.rm = TRUE),
    ETTR_scale = rowMeans(across(all_of(ETTR_items)), na.rm = TRUE)
  )

Create Attachment Groups

A lower/higher attachment grouping variable was created for the planned 2 x 2 ANOVA models. Participants with attachment scores at or below the sample median were assigned to the Lower group, and participants above the sample median were assigned to the Higher group.

Show code 
# Create median values for the attachment scale scores
aas_total_median <- median(study_data$aas_total_scale, na.rm = TRUE)
aas_close_median <- median(study_data$aas_close_scale, na.rm = TRUE)
aas_depend_median <- median(study_data$aas_depend_scale, na.rm = TRUE)
aas_anxiety_median <- median(study_data$aas_anxiety_scale, na.rm = TRUE)

# Create median-split attachment groups
study_data <- study_data %>%
  mutate(
    aas_total_group = if_else(aas_total_scale <= aas_total_median, "Lower attachment security", "Higher attachment security"),
    aas_total_group = factor(aas_total_group, levels = c("Lower attachment security", "Higher attachment security")),
    
    aas_close_group = if_else(aas_close_scale <= aas_close_median, "Lower closeness security", "Higher closeness security"),
    aas_close_group = factor(aas_close_group, levels = c("Lower closeness security", "Higher closeness security")),
    
    aas_depend_group = if_else(aas_depend_scale <= aas_depend_median, "Lower dependence security", "Higher dependence security"),
    aas_depend_group = factor(aas_depend_group, levels = c("Lower dependence security", "Higher dependence security")),
    
    aas_anxiety_group = if_else(aas_anxiety_scale <= aas_anxiety_median, "Lower anxiety security", "Higher anxiety security"),
    aas_anxiety_group = factor(aas_anxiety_group, levels = c("Lower anxiety security", "Higher anxiety security"))
  )

# Check final attachment group sizes
study_data %>%
  count(aas_total_group) %>%
  knitr::kable()

Check Scale Reliability

Internal consistency was estimated for social attraction, attachment security, and perceived compatibility scales before the scale scores were used in the primary analyses.

Show code 
# Create item-only data frames for each scale
IAS_item_df <- study_data %>% select(all_of(IAS_items))
aas_close_item_df <- study_data %>% select(all_of(aas_close_items))
aas_depend_item_df <- study_data %>% select(all_of(aas_depend_items))
aas_anxiety_item_df <- study_data %>% select(all_of(aas_anxiety_items))
aas_total_item_df <- study_data %>% select(all_of(aas_total_items))
ETTR_item_df <- study_data %>% select(all_of(ETTR_items))

# Compute internal consistency estimates
IAS_alpha <- psych::alpha(IAS_item_df)
IAS_omega <- psych::omega(IAS_item_df, plot = FALSE)

aas_close_alpha <- psych::alpha(aas_close_item_df)
aas_close_omega <- psych::omega(aas_close_item_df, plot = FALSE)

aas_depend_alpha <- psych::alpha(aas_depend_item_df)
aas_depend_omega <- psych::omega(aas_depend_item_df, plot = FALSE)

aas_anxiety_alpha <- psych::alpha(aas_anxiety_item_df)
aas_anxiety_omega <- psych::omega(aas_anxiety_item_df, plot = FALSE)

aas_total_alpha <- psych::alpha(aas_total_item_df)
aas_total_omega <- psych::omega(aas_total_item_df, plot = FALSE)

ETTR_alpha <- psych::alpha(ETTR_item_df)
ETTR_omega <- psych::omega(ETTR_item_df, plot = FALSE)

# Print only alpha and omega coefficients
tibble(
  scale = c("Social Attraction", "AAS Close Security", "AAS Depend Security", "AAS Anxiety Security", "AAS Total Security", "Relationship Expectation"),
  alpha = c(IAS_alpha$total$raw_alpha, aas_close_alpha$total$raw_alpha, aas_depend_alpha$total$raw_alpha, aas_anxiety_alpha$total$raw_alpha, aas_total_alpha$total$raw_alpha, ETTR_alpha$total$raw_alpha),
  omega = c(IAS_omega$omega.tot, aas_close_omega$omega.tot, aas_depend_omega$omega.tot, aas_anxiety_omega$omega.tot, aas_total_omega$omega.tot, ETTR_omega$omega.tot)
) %>%
  knitr::kable()
scale alpha omega

AAS Anxiety Security 0.8796060 0.9251593

Primary Analyses

This section reports the primary analyses used to test whether communication condition, attachment securirty, and their interaction predicted social attraction and perceived compatibility scores.

A series of 2 x 2 ANOVAs tested whether social attraction and perceived compatibility differed by communication condition, attachment security subscale (total attachment security, closeness, dependence, and anxiety) and their interaction. Each subscale was tested as a seperate moderator.

Perceived Compatibility (ETTR) Model 1: Total Attachment Security

A 2 x 2 ANOVA tested whether perceived compatibility scores differed by communication condition, total attachment security group, and the communication condition x total attachment security group interaction.

Show code 
# 2x2 between-subjects ANOVA predicting relationship expectation scores
# DV: ETTR_scale
# Factors: condition and aas_total_group
a1_ETTR_total <- afex::aov_ez(
  id = "id",
  dv = "ETTR_scale",
  between = c("condition", "aas_total_group"),
  data = study_data
)

# Print the ANOVA table
a1_ETTR_total
Anova Table (Type 3 tests)

Response: ETTR_scale
                     Effect    df  MSE         F  ges p.value
1                 condition 1, 91 0.75 32.97 *** .266   <.001
2           aas_total_group 1, 91 0.75      1.49 .016    .225
3 condition:aas_total_group 1, 91 0.75      0.17 .002    .680
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '+' 0.1 ' ' 1

The ANOVA table reports the main effect of communication profile condition, the main effect of total attchment security group, and the communication condition x total attachment security group interaction for perceived compatibility scores.

Figures

This section creates the figures used to visualize the primary 2 x 2 ANOVA results. The figures are based on the estimated cell means from the ANOVA model.

Perceived Compatibility (ETTR) Interaction Plot: Total Attachment Security

Show code 
p_ETTR_total_bar <- ggplot(
  as.data.frame(emmeans(a1_ETTR_total, ~ condition * aas_total_group)),
  aes(
    x = condition,
    y = emmean,
    fill = aas_total_group
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.65),
    width = 0.55,
    color = "white"
  ) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(
      ymin = lower.CL,
      ymax = upper.CL
    ),
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.65),
    width = 0.12,
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_text(
  aes(label = round(emmean, 2)),
  position = position_dodge(width = 0.65),
  vjust = -0.5,
  size = 4
) +
  labs(
    x = "Communication Condition",
    y = "Mean Relationship Expectation Score",
    fill = "Total Attachment Security"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Lower attachment security" = "#FFC0CB",  # YOU CAN CHANGE THESE TWO HEX VALUES TO MATCH YOUR POSTER! 
      "Higher attachment security" = "#89CFF0"  # YOU CAN CHANGE THESE TWO HEX VALUES TO MATCH YOUR POSTER! 
    )
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = 1:6
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(
    ylim = c(1, 6)
  ) +
  theme_classic(
    base_size = 14
  ) + 
  theme(legend.position = c(0.5, 0.98),
        legend.justification = c(0.5,1),
        legend.background = element_blank())

p_ETTR_total_bar

The figure shows estimated perceived compatibility (ETTR) scores by communication condition and total attachment security group. Error bars represent 95% confidence intervals.

Results Summary

The primary analyses assessed whether communication profile condition, attachment security group (and its sub-scales), and their interaction predicted social attraction (IAS) and perceived compatibility (ETTR) scores. Overall, participants exposed to the high communication profile reported higher social attraction and perceived compatibility than those in the low communication condition. Across the series of 2 x 2 ANOVA models, communication condition displayed a significant pattern of higher scores for both measures of romantic preference, which suggests open communication may be an important valued characteristic when discussing romantic evaluations.

In contrast, attachment security sub-scales showed more variable effects, with some significant main effects for social attraction, but not for perceived compatibility. Additionally, no interaction effects were found between communication condition and any attachment security sub-scale for either attraction or perceived compatibility, which indicates attachment security did not moderate the effects of communication condition on social attraction or perceived compatibility. The estimated means and interaction plots above provide the full analyses output and allow for visualization of the pattern of results for each outcome.

## Introduction / Study Overview

*This reproducible report documents the data preparation, variable construction, descriptive statistics, primary analyses, and figures for this study.*

*The report is intended to accompany a manuscript-style research paper. The report cannot substitute the full paper itself. Rather, this displays a transparent record of the reported results, using a reproducible Quarto workflow.*

This study *examined whether communication style and attachment security influence social attraction and perceived relationship compatibility, and their interaction.*

*The design included one manipulated independent variable and one quasi-categorical moderator :*

*- communication condition: low communication profile versus high communication profile*

*- attachment security: lower attachment security versus higher attachment security*

*The dependent variables were social attraction scores and perceived compatibility scores.*

*The primary analyses tested whether communication condition, attachment security, and their interaction predicted social attraction and perceived compatibility.*

*It was predicted that participants in the high communication condition would report greater social attraction and perceived compatibility than those in the low communication condition. Furthermore, attachment security was predicted to moderate this effect, such that individuals with higher attachment security would report greater attraction and compatibility in response to the high communication profile; whereas individuals with lower attachment security would show less variation in responses across the communication profiles.*

### Reverse-Code Scale Items

*Items requiring reverse coding were adjusted prior to scale scores being computed. Given that this study included three Likert scales with different response ranges, reverse-coded items were created by subtracting each item response from the respective scale maximum plus one (i.e., 8 for 1-7 scales and 7 for 1-6 scales).*

```{r}
#| label: reverse_code_items
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

study_data <- study_data %>%
  mutate(
    IAS_3r = 8 - IAS_3,
    IAS_4r = 8 - IAS_4,
    IAS_5r = 8 - IAS_5,
    
    ETTR_2r  = 7 - ETTR_2,
    ETTR_5r  = 7 - ETTR_5,
    ETTR_7r  = 7 - ETTR_7,
    ETTR_10r = 7 - ETTR_10,
    ETTR_13r = 7 - ETTR_13,
    ETTR_16r = 7 - ETTR_16,
    ETTR_18r = 7 - ETTR_18,
    
    AAS_8r  = 6 - AAS_8,
    AAS_13r = 6 - AAS_13,
    AAS_17r = 6 - AAS_17,
    AAS_2r  = 6 - AAS_2,
    AAS_16r = 6 - AAS_16,
    AAS_18r = 6 - AAS_18,
    
    AAS_3r  = 6 - AAS_3,
    AAS_4r  = 6 - AAS_4,
    AAS_9r  = 6 - AAS_9,
    AAS_10r = 6 - AAS_10,
    AAS_11r = 6 - AAS_11,
    AAS_15r = 6 - AAS_15
  )
```

### Check Reverse Coding

```{r}
#| label: check_reverse_coding
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

study_data %>%
  select(IAS_3,IAS_3r, ETTR_2, ETTR_2r, AAS_3, AAS_3r) %>%
  head(10) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

*The reverse-coding check shows examples of original and reverse-coded item pairs. These checks confirm that reverse-coded variables were created before scale scores were computed.*

### Create Scale Scores

*Scale item lists were defined and used to compute attachment security, social attraction, and perceived compatibility scores.*

*Note: AAS items were reverse-scored so that all attachment scale scores point in a positive direction. Higher scores indicate more adaptive attachment-related outcomes. Specifically, higher total AAS scores indicate higher overall attachment security, higher closeness scores indicate greater comfort with closeness, higher dependence scores indicate greater comfort depending on others, and higher anxiety-security scores indicate lower attachment anxiety.*

```{r}
#| label: create_scale_scores
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Define IAS social attraction items
IAS_items <- c("IAS_1", "IAS_2", "IAS_3r", "IAS_4r", "IAS_5r", "IAS_6")

# Define revised AAS close, depend, and anxiety-security items
aas_close_items <- c("AAS_1", "AAS_6", "AAS_8r", "AAS_12", "AAS_13r", "AAS_17r")

aas_depend_items <- c("AAS_2r", "AAS_5", "AAS_7", "AAS_14", "AAS_16r", "AAS_18r")

aas_anxiety_items <- c("AAS_3r", "AAS_4r", "AAS_9r", "AAS_10r", "AAS_11r", "AAS_15r")

aas_total_items <- c(aas_close_items, aas_depend_items, aas_anxiety_items)

# Define ETRR relationship expectation items
ETTR_items <- c("ETTR_1", "ETTR_2r", "ETTR_3", "ETTR_4", "ETTR_5r", "ETTR_6", 
                "ETTR_7r", "ETTR_8", "ETTR_9", "ETTR_10r", "ETTR_11", "ETTR_12", 
                "ETTR_13r", "ETTR_14", "ETTR_15", "ETTR_16r", "ETTR_17", "ETTR_18r", "ETTR_19")

study_data <- study_data %>%
  mutate(
    IAS_scale = rowMeans(across(all_of(IAS_items)), na.rm = TRUE),
    aas_close_scale = rowMeans(across(all_of(aas_close_items)), na.rm = TRUE),
    aas_depend_scale = rowMeans(across(all_of(aas_depend_items)), na.rm = TRUE),
    aas_anxiety_scale = rowMeans(across(all_of(aas_anxiety_items)), na.rm = TRUE),
    aas_total_scale = rowMeans(across(all_of(aas_total_items)), na.rm = TRUE),
    ETTR_scale = rowMeans(across(all_of(ETTR_items)), na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

### Check Scale Scores

```{r}
#| label: check_scale_scores
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

study_data %>%
  select(IAS_scale, aas_close_scale, aas_depend_scale, aas_anxiety_scale, aas_total_scale, ETTR_scale) %>%
  summary()

study_data %>%
  summarise(
    IAS_missing = mean(is.na(IAS_scale)),
    aas_close_missing = mean(is.na(aas_close_scale)),
    aas_depend_missing = mean(is.na(aas_depend_scale)),
    aas_anxiety_missing = mean(is.na(aas_anxiety_scale)),
    aas_total_missing = mean(is.na(aas_total_scale)),
    ETTR_missing = mean(is.na(ETTR_scale))
  ) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

*The scale-score checks confirm the computed scale scores fall within the expected response range and also include whether any scale scores are missing.*

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Create Attachment Groups

*A lower/higher attachment grouping variable was created for the planned 2 x 2 ANOVA models. Participants with attachment scores at or below the sample median were assigned to the Lower group, and participants above the sample median were assigned to the Higher group.*

```{r}
#| label: create_attachment_groups
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Create median values for the attachment scale scores
aas_total_median <- median(study_data$aas_total_scale, na.rm = TRUE)
aas_close_median <- median(study_data$aas_close_scale, na.rm = TRUE)
aas_depend_median <- median(study_data$aas_depend_scale, na.rm = TRUE)
aas_anxiety_median <- median(study_data$aas_anxiety_scale, na.rm = TRUE)

# Create median-split attachment groups
study_data <- study_data %>%
  mutate(
    aas_total_group = if_else(aas_total_scale <= aas_total_median, "Lower attachment security", "Higher attachment security"),
    aas_total_group = factor(aas_total_group, levels = c("Lower attachment security", "Higher attachment security")),
    
    aas_close_group = if_else(aas_close_scale <= aas_close_median, "Lower closeness security", "Higher closeness security"),
    aas_close_group = factor(aas_close_group, levels = c("Lower closeness security", "Higher closeness security")),
    
    aas_depend_group = if_else(aas_depend_scale <= aas_depend_median, "Lower dependence security", "Higher dependence security"),
    aas_depend_group = factor(aas_depend_group, levels = c("Lower dependence security", "Higher dependence security")),
    
    aas_anxiety_group = if_else(aas_anxiety_scale <= aas_anxiety_median, "Lower anxiety security", "Higher anxiety security"),
    aas_anxiety_group = factor(aas_anxiety_group, levels = c("Lower anxiety security", "Higher anxiety security"))
  )

# Check final attachment group sizes
study_data %>%
  count(aas_total_group) %>%
  knitr::kable()

study_data %>%
  count(aas_close_group) %>%
  knitr::kable()

study_data %>%
  count(aas_depend_group) %>%
  knitr::kable()

study_data %>%
  count(aas_anxiety_group) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

*Median splits were created for each of the attachment security subscales: total attachment, dependence, anxiety, and closeness security, which were then used in the primary ANOVA models. The output reports the median value used for the split and the number of participants assigned to each attachment group within each sub-scale.*

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Check Scale Reliability

*Internal consistency was estimated for social attraction, attachment security, and perceived compatibility scales before the scale scores were used in the primary analyses.*

```{r}
#| label: reliability_checks
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Create item-only data frames for each scale
IAS_item_df <- study_data %>% select(all_of(IAS_items))
aas_close_item_df <- study_data %>% select(all_of(aas_close_items))
aas_depend_item_df <- study_data %>% select(all_of(aas_depend_items))
aas_anxiety_item_df <- study_data %>% select(all_of(aas_anxiety_items))
aas_total_item_df <- study_data %>% select(all_of(aas_total_items))
ETTR_item_df <- study_data %>% select(all_of(ETTR_items))

# Compute internal consistency estimates
IAS_alpha <- psych::alpha(IAS_item_df)
IAS_omega <- psych::omega(IAS_item_df, plot = FALSE)

aas_close_alpha <- psych::alpha(aas_close_item_df)
aas_close_omega <- psych::omega(aas_close_item_df, plot = FALSE)

aas_depend_alpha <- psych::alpha(aas_depend_item_df)
aas_depend_omega <- psych::omega(aas_depend_item_df, plot = FALSE)

aas_anxiety_alpha <- psych::alpha(aas_anxiety_item_df)
aas_anxiety_omega <- psych::omega(aas_anxiety_item_df, plot = FALSE)

aas_total_alpha <- psych::alpha(aas_total_item_df)
aas_total_omega <- psych::omega(aas_total_item_df, plot = FALSE)

ETTR_alpha <- psych::alpha(ETTR_item_df)
ETTR_omega <- psych::omega(ETTR_item_df, plot = FALSE)

# Print only alpha and omega coefficients
tibble(
  scale = c("Social Attraction", "AAS Close Security", "AAS Depend Security", "AAS Anxiety Security", "AAS Total Security", "Relationship Expectation"),
  alpha = c(IAS_alpha$total$raw_alpha, aas_close_alpha$total$raw_alpha, aas_depend_alpha$total$raw_alpha, aas_anxiety_alpha$total$raw_alpha, aas_total_alpha$total$raw_alpha, ETTR_alpha$total$raw_alpha),
  omega = c(IAS_omega$omega.tot, aas_close_omega$omega.tot, aas_depend_omega$omega.tot, aas_anxiety_omega$omega.tot, aas_total_omega$omega.tot, ETTR_omega$omega.tot)
) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

*The reliability table reports Cronbach's alpha and McDonald's omega for each scale used in the analysis.*

## Primary Analyses

*This section reports the primary analyses used to test whether communication condition, attachment securirty, and their interaction predicted social attraction and perceived compatibility scores.*

*A series of 2 x 2 ANOVAs tested whether social attraction and perceived compatibility differed by communication condition, attachment security subscale (total attachment security, closeness, dependence, and anxiety) and their interaction. Each subscale was tested as a seperate moderator.*

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Perceived Compatibility (ETTR) Model 1: Total Attachment Security

*A 2 x 2 ANOVA tested whether perceived compatibility scores differed by communication condition, total attachment security group, and the communication condition x total attachment security group interaction.*

```{r}
#| label: anova_relationship_expectation_total_attachment
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# 2x2 between-subjects ANOVA predicting relationship expectation scores
# DV: ETTR_scale
# Factors: condition and aas_total_group
a1_ETTR_total <- afex::aov_ez(
  id = "id",
  dv = "ETTR_scale",
  between = c("condition", "aas_total_group"),
  data = study_data
)

# Print the ANOVA table
a1_ETTR_total
```

*The ANOVA table reports the main effect of communication profile condition, the main effect of total attchment security group, and the communication condition x total attachment security group interaction for perceived compatibility scores.*

### Estimated Means for Perceived Compatibility (ETTR): Total Attachment Security

```{r}
#| label: estimated_means_relationship_expectation_total_attachment
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

emmeans(a1_ETTR_total, ~ condition)

emmeans(a1_ETTR_total, ~ aas_total_group)

emmeans(a1_ETTR_total, ~ condition * aas_total_group)
```

*The estimated means show the perceived compatibility score pattern across communication condition, total attachment security group, and the four communication x total attachment security combinations (cell means).*

## Figures

*This section creates the figures used to visualize the primary 2 x 2 ANOVA results. The figures are based on the estimated cell means from the ANOVA model.*

### Perceived Compatibility (ETTR) Interaction Plot: Total Attachment Security

```{r}
#| label: interaction_plot_relationship_expectation_total_attachment
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

p_ETTR_total_bar <- ggplot(
  as.data.frame(emmeans(a1_ETTR_total, ~ condition * aas_total_group)),
  aes(
    x = condition,
    y = emmean,
    fill = aas_total_group
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.65),
    width = 0.55,
    color = "white"
  ) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(
      ymin = lower.CL,
      ymax = upper.CL
    ),
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.65),
    width = 0.12,
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_text(
  aes(label = round(emmean, 2)),
  position = position_dodge(width = 0.65),
  vjust = -0.5,
  size = 4
) +
  labs(
    x = "Communication Condition",
    y = "Mean Relationship Expectation Score",
    fill = "Total Attachment Security"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Lower attachment security" = "#FFC0CB",  # YOU CAN CHANGE THESE TWO HEX VALUES TO MATCH YOUR POSTER! 
      "Higher attachment security" = "#89CFF0"  # YOU CAN CHANGE THESE TWO HEX VALUES TO MATCH YOUR POSTER! 
    )
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = 1:6
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(
    ylim = c(1, 6)
  ) +
  theme_classic(
    base_size = 14
  ) + 
  theme(legend.position = c(0.5, 0.98),
        legend.justification = c(0.5,1),
        legend.background = element_blank())

p_ETTR_total_bar
```

*The figure shows estimated perceived compatibility (ETTR) scores by communication condition and total attachment security group. Error bars represent 95% confidence intervals.*

```{r}
    ylim = c(1, 7)
  ) +
  theme_classic(
    base_size = 14
  ) + 
  theme(legend.position = c(0.5, 0.98),
        legend.justification = c(0.5,1),
        legend.background = element_blank())

p_IAS_total_bar
print(p_IAS_total_bar)
```

*The figure shows estimated social attraction (IAS) scores by communication condition and total attachment security group. Error bars represent 95% confidence intervals.*

## Results Summary

*The primary analyses assessed whether communication profile condition, attachment security group (and its sub-scales), and their interaction predicted social attraction (IAS) and perceived compatibility (ETTR) scores. Overall, participants exposed to the high communication profile reported higher social attraction and perceived compatibility than those in the low communication condition. Across the series of 2 x 2 ANOVA models, communication condition displayed a significant pattern of higher scores for both measures of romantic preference, which suggests open communication may be an important valued characteristic when discussing romantic evaluations.*

*In contrast, attachment security sub-scales showed more variable effects, with some significant main effects for social attraction, but not for perceived compatibility. Additionally, no interaction effects were found between communication condition and any attachment security sub-scale for either attraction or perceived compatibility, which indicates attachment security did not moderate the effects of communication condition on social attraction or perceived compatibility. The estimated means and interaction plots above provide the full analyses output and allow for visualization of the pattern of results for each outcome.*
